paragraphs.text: XVII. POEMS.
I. GENESIS.
In the beginning the Lord set heaven and earth in place,
for the earth was formless and hidden beneath the flood,
and the boundless God moved over the vast waters
while chaos and black darkness dimmed all things.
As he ordered these to be parted at the hinge of the world, he spoke:
“Let there be light,” and all things shone out in a bright world.
When the Lord had completed the works of the first day,
he founded the vault of heaven, white with newborn clouds;
the boundless sea received its wandering shores,
sweeping in many rivers with its mighty currents.
The third golden daylight uncovered the face of the lands;
soon the dry ground is given a name and called earth;
flowering shoots spring up over the windy plains,
and fruit-bearing boughs bend down their arms together.
On the fourth day he brings forth the moon with the lamp of the sun
and fashions the stars, gleaming with trembling light;
these elements he gave as signs to the world below,
to teach the seasons that must change through their various risings.
On the fifth day the flowing rivers receive the fish,
and birds of every kind hang their wings in the air.
On the sixth the Father makes the cold serpents slither in their coils
and spreads herds of four-footed beasts over all the fields,
and he commanded all things to increase everywhere with manifold
offspring, and to roam and graze over the boundless lands.
When divine power had established these things by its command,
seeing that a ruler was lacking for the things of the world,
he says: “Let us make man exactly in the likeness
of our own countenance, to reign over the whole world.”
And though he could have composed him with a single word,
yet he deigned to mould him with his own holy right hand,
and from his divine breast he breathes into the senseless breast.
After he saw him formed as if in his own image,
he judged that, alone, the man would brood on gnawing cares.
At once he bathes his eyes in refreshing sleep,
so that a woman might be gently formed from a rib drawn out,
and her substance might strengthen her limbs with a twofold mixture.
She is given the name of life, which is called Eve.
Therefore children, as is the custom, leave their parents
and cling to their spouses once they have set up their homes.
On the seventh day God rested at the end of his works,
appointing it as hallowed for the joys of the age to come.
Then, when the throngs of living creatures had been presented in order,
to each one by one a name that endures is given
by Adam, skilful with the wisdom granted to him.
God deigns to address him, and Eve joined with him:
“Increase by manifold childbearing for times to come,
so that heaven and earth may be full of your offspring;
and as my heirs, pluck the various fruits
which the groves and fields yield from their rich soil.”
When he had said this, paradise is furnished as a joyful hall
and beholds the light of the first sun.
Among these grows a tree with deadly fruit,
producing the mingled taste of life and death.
In the midst of the dwellings flows a river in a pure stream,
which waters the splendid gardens with its liquid waves
and from its welling source divides into four courses.
The Pishon, exceedingly rich, surges with gold-bearing waters
and wears down glittering gems in its roaring flood:
green prase is the name of one, the other is the blazing carbuncle;
and with its clear shallows it laps the land of Havilah.
After it the Gihon flows on and enriches the Ethiopians.
The third is the Tigris, joined to the pleasant Euphrates,
cutting its separate furrow through Assyria with its swift stream.
Here Adam is set as keeper with his faithful wife,
and as a workman he is instructed by the Thunderer's voice in these words:
“Do not be afraid, both of you, to pluck the permitted fruits
which the unpruned grove has brought forth on its leafy boughs;
only take care that you do not by chance pick the harmful fruit
which flourishes with a twofold juice for separate purposes.”
Meanwhile deep night still held them blind,
and no garment yet covered their newly formed limbs.
Among these dwellings and gardens of mellow berries,
foaming at the mouth and surpassing all animals in cunning,
the snake crept silently in its cold coils;
turning over livid lies in his biting mind,
he tests the soft heart within the woman's breast:
“Tell me, why do you fear the happy fruit of the apple tree?
Has God not hallowed all the fruits that are known?
If you are eager to pluck honeyed food from them,
a golden world will return from the star-bearing pole.”
She refuses, and fears to touch the forbidden boughs;
but still her heart is overcome by weakness of judgment.
As soon as she bit the mellow fruit with her snowy tooth,
a clear sky shone out, stained by no cloud.
Then the taste, putting its allure into her honeyed throat,
drove her to bring the gift to her unsuspecting husband.
As soon as he took it, the night was wiped away, and their eyes
flashed bright and clear as the world gleamed.
So when each of them looked upon the naked body
and they saw their shameful parts, they shaded them with fig leaves.
Then, as the sun's light was setting, they chanced to recognize the sound
of the Lord, and trembling they made for hidden places.
Then the Lord of heaven addresses the sorrowful Adam:
“Tell me, where are you now?” He answered thus as a suppliant:
“O Lord, at your words I tremble with a fearful heart,
great one, and naked I am worn down by chilling fear.”
Then the Lord: “Who gave you the harmful fruit?”
“The woman gave it,” he says, telling how at once her eyes,
flooded with gleaming day, had seen the clear sky
and the sun and the stars of heaven shine out for her.
At once God's anger terrifies the troubled Eve,
as the Most High seeks the author of the forbidden deed.
Upon this she reveals: “Persuaded by the speaking serpent,
I took it, through deceiving guile and coaxing entreaty;
for, weaving his words with viper's poisons,
he told me that these were sweeter than all fruits.”
At once the Almighty condemns the serpent's deeds,
commanding all to look upon the hated monster:
henceforth to crawl on outstretched breast, and to chew
the soil with his bite; and in a war that would last for all time
between human senses and himself as he glides along,
he would creep prone with head cast down behind men's legs,
so that man might tread on him as he slithers and presses close.
The woman, wretchedly deceived by treacherous persuasion,
is commanded to bring forth her offspring in hard peril
and to bear servitude to her husband with devotion.
“But you, to whom your wife's counsel seemed true,
she who yielded, overcome, to the cruel serpent,
you will lament your wretched toil through long ages;
for instead of a crop of wheaten harvest there will spring up for you
the thistle and the thornbush with its many sharp spikes,
so that with weary body and sorrowful heart
your anxious bread will cost you many sighs,
until, in the setting time of death that comes,
you are returned to the lowly earth from which you bear your body.”
This done, the Lord makes the trembling pair weary of life,
and drives them, cast down, far from the sacred gardens,
and sets them facing away and bars them out with fire between,
in which the Cherub is whirled about in a swift blaze,
while the hot blade seethes and rolls out flames.
For them the Lord, lest their limbs grow stiff with numbing cold,
stitched together skins stripped from [?] cattle,
covering their naked limbs with warm garments.
So when faithful Adam perceived that he was now
a husband in marriage, he gives his wife the name
of beloved mother. The two sons who were born of his seed
their father at once names with different titles.
This one is named Cain, and with him is joined Abel:
the one kept the harmless sheep with great care,
while the other turned the earth with the curved plough.
When they brought their gifts to the everlasting Thunderer,
they offered unlike fruits, as their minds persuaded them.
For the first offered what had sprung from the fertile clods;
but the other devotes himself with a gentle lamb,
bearing in his hand pure entrails and snowy fat.
And at once the pious offering pleases the Lord as he looks upon it.
Because of this Cain burned with chill anger.
God, deigning to address him, begins thus:
“Tell me, if you live rightly and discern what is harmful,
could you not live clean of the guilt you have incurred?
Cease plotting your brother's ruin in your biting mind,
for he will bow his neck to you, subject to you as to a lord.”
Yet not broken by these words, he leads his brother out to the fields,
and when he saw him caught on the lonely grass,
he treacherously crushes his innocent throat with both hands.
The Lord, watching this deed from high heaven,
asks where on earth Abel might be.
He denies that he has been appointed his brother's keeper.
To him God declares: “Does not the voice of his blood
sound, sent to me, and rise up to the lofty sky?
Know, then, what awaits you for so great a crime:
the earth which has just been soaked with your brother's blood,
cursed, will refuse you, hateful as you are, the seeds entrusted to it,
and with its plants consumed will bring forth no fruit,
so that, numb, your limbs knocking together with violent trembling …
II. SODOM.
Already almighty God had blotted out the crimes of the first age
with an avenging flood, with all the waters
that the sky scatters, the earth vomits forth and the sea spits out;
and having covenanted to decree no more punishments
by watery destruction, whenever the air should bring on a storm,
he had appointed the many-coloured bow to curb the rains,
marking the clouds with a purple and green border,
called by the name of Iris, the very clasp of the storm clouds.
But impiety returned together with the second race
of men, and a new age of evil sprouted again,
now allotted not rains for its punishment, but fires.
Thus the land of Sodom deserved to be burned with blazing
dews, and to foreshadow signs of the end to come.
There savage lust, the enemy of shame,
stood as law, so that a forewarned stranger would flee it,
preferring rather, at Scythian altars or at the altars of Busiris,
to seek death in sacrifice, or to yield his blood
to the Bebrycian gauntlet and glut the Libyan wrestling grounds;
preferring even to take on new shapes through Circe's cups
rather than lose his violated sex at Sodom.
Monstrous unions battered heaven with outrage,
nature in equal incest rebelling against its own kind,
and the name of man violated together with his body.
But God, who foresees all things, at an appointed time
judges the unjust, patient until the long age of crime,
having squandered its time for amendment, had compelled his wrath.
And now the day of vengeance was at hand. Two sent from the heavenly host,
young men in appearance, both of them angelic spirits
in divine service, as the Lord's commands directed,
come to Sodom. There, of the stock of the pious,
Lot, a newcomer, a wise settler, fair and just,
alone remembered God: often a useful tree
lies hidden in wild woods, its fruit like a stranger there.
He was then sitting before the gate (the heavenly ones had scarcely
reached the walls), and though unaware that they were divine, of his own accord
he calls to them, greets them, honours them with a father's reverence,
and invites them to his house, though they meant to lodge far off;
having prevailed with long entreaties, he provides the pious pledges of the table
and every kind service with friendly zeal.
Night had given rest, and the next day had dispelled the night,
when Sodom clamours at the doors with its shameful law.
Lot, a suppliant, faces them: “Let not ill-fed lust
inflame you, young men, to defile these youths.
What is this indulgence in which begetting is void, and seed spent in vain?
In which no living creatures mate — not those that dwell in dens,
not those returning to their stalls, not those gaping beneath the waters,
nor those that hang near the clouds on the rhythm of their wings,
nor those that glide over the earth with drawn-out bodies.
Every kind begets by striving, and the female is the mate
of all, and no one ever has a mother but a female.
Now if youthful passion longs to lay waste to modesty,
I have two daughters within, of marriageable age,
their maidenhood swelling in flower, already ripe for harvest,
a desire worthy of men; wherever your will may lead,
I, their father, hand them over, and will pay with my grief for my guests.”
To this the mad crowd: “Who are you, how great, and where from,
that you lord it over our minds and lay down laws?
A newcomer, not a ruler, you weigh out the acres of Sodom.
Now then, you yourself shall pay for what our desire wants
in place of daughters and guests: one man is enough for all.”
No sooner said than done: the raging crowd brooks no delay.
As a turbulent torrent rolls on in its wintry onrush
and carries countless streams of brooks in a single course,
if any tree there is struck by the rushing waters,
it will not last long; as far as its root allows
its hairy tendrils hold out for a while; but when beneath it
it loses the eaten-away ground and hangs with its trunk undermined,
swaying this way and that, it defers its certain fall.
Just so Lot, in the midst of the crowd's whirlpool,
was tottering, almost overcome; but divine power
came to his aid: the angelic young men snatched him from the threshold
and brought him back into the house; and the mad crowd there
they punish meanwhile with loss of sight, as a foretaste of punishment.
Then they disclose God's decrees: that a fitting punishment
from heaven was at hand for Sodom, and that Lot had earned salvation
by right of his justice: “Why then do you not gird yourself
to hasten your flight from here, and lead out likewise any
of your kin you have? For we are now bringing destruction on the city.”
Lot quickly speaks to his sons-in-law, but the hard minds of men
disdained to believe the warning and laughed at his fear.
Soon, at the hour when light first tries to rend the darkness
and the face of the sky is two-coloured with night and day,
the young men pressed to lead the Chaldean family
out of Sodom and bestow salvation on the just household:
“Come, Lot, rise up, take your wife
and your two daughters, and go hence as an exile,
ahead of Sodom's punishment.” With friendly hands, too,
they lead the trembling ones out, and there give their remaining commands:
“Save your life, Lot, and do not think to turn your gaze
backward, nor to halt the steps you have begun;
hurry to the mountain.” Lot feared to climb the heights
with slow steps, lest the heavenly wrath
overwhelm them first; he begins to ask for another haven,
a small city which he had seen opposite.
“Let our flight be here,” he says; “surely it scarcely rises with walls,
it is not far, nor is it great to ask.” They favoured the frightened man
and granted the safety of that city too;
hence the barbarian tongue knows the place by the name of Zoar.
Then Lot enters Zoar, and at the same moment the sun rises,
the last indeed for Sodom; already seething with fires,
in its anger it had armed its rays with all its flame.
A rival darkness creeps in beneath, trying to shut in the light
and to weave thick masses into the confounded sky.
Smoking clouds gather, a strange rain rushes down,
sulphur with flames; chaos blazes, the upper sky seethes,
the scorched air crackles with liquid fires.
From this the fable has drawn its false fame from the truth:
that the offspring of the Sun longed for his father's chariot,
and that the tender boy could not rein in the proud
horses of the Sun, and the world burned; that the charioteer
was then snatched away by a thunderbolt, and his sisters were transformed for their unlawful lament.
Let the Eridanus see to it, whether any poplar grows white there,
whether any more tuneful bird puts on its plumes there in old age.
Here the marvels of a changed form mourn in another way.
For his companion and wife — alas, ill-obedient to the law even then —
a woman, hearing the rumblings of the divine heaven,
in vain twisted her bold eyes behind her,
never to tell what she had seen; and at once, right there,
changed into brittle salt, she stood, herself her own tomb
and herself her own image, keeping a shape without a body.
For she endures even now, at her bare post under the open sky,
neither dissolved by rains, nor wasted by decay, nor broken by winds;
moreover, if any stranger mutilates her form,
at once she fills up the wounds from her own supply.
And it is said that, still living in another body now, her sex
discharges its customary monthly courses with bountiful blood.
And now nowhere are the cities of Sodom, nowhere the impious people;
the whole region is a pyre: here with the black horror of embers,
there with the grey decay of ashes, the burning leaves its marks.
No one ploughs the clods, pitch-black with soot; it would be in vain.
Gone is that former beauty which Lot, looking out over it
when he parted from his uncle, had chosen as rich fields.
Even if any half-dead acres there attempt the glad
riches of autumn, pears, peaches and all kinds of apples readily
promise the eyes that they are of the best,
until you long to pick them: for at once, at the revealing touch,
the deceit of the empty fruit dissolves into ash.
Thus, with heaven and earth alike buried there,
not even the sea lives; death is the sea, the sea's very peace,
for it stirs no waves through panting surges,
it never sighs even at its native south wind,
and it cannot bring forth from its depths any race of creatures,
scaly-skinned or smooth-skinned or fenced in a shell,
or the ridged conch, or that which is shut within a double hinge.
Bitumen alone reaps its own harvest there,
the soot of the burnt sea, which a lively heat,
cooking beneath the waters with the heat of sulphur and salt,
tempers, giving the land a sea-pitch to possess.
At its proper season the rich slime of the burnt water
is borne in, and a skin of black foam is woven
over the waters. Those whose trade it is to gather this ware put in,
and tilt their light skiffs, balancing their sides,
to coax the vein, once it has been laid on, to climb aboard;
for, lifting itself of its own accord, it will give itself to the idle
vessel and would sink it with its lavish gift,
unless it touches the cloth with which a woman covers her monthly flow.
Behold, another marvel of that sea is noted from the disaster:
everything there floats against its will; nature has withdrawn
the law fixed for bodies that sink. Indeed, if you set
a lighted lamp afloat, while the breath of fire is in it,
the tip of the flame will sail; but if the flame is put out,
the wreck of the light will go down beneath the waters.
These punishments of Sodom and Gomorrah, marked out for the ages,
will teach the unjust nations, whose hard hearts
have abandoned the fear of God, to revere the laws of heaven
and to hope in the one Lord of all things.
III. ON JONAH.
After Sodom and Gomorrah, living funerals for all time,
and the punishing fires marked by the decay of ashes,
and the fruits that grow in vain, for the eyes alone,
and likewise the death of the sea there, and the salt,
if a human being is anything who keeps her punishment in a changed body —
after all this, another shower of fiery rain from above had almost been brought down
by the city of Nineveh, which had strayed from the path of fairness and justice.
For what fear has a perverted mind? All
lessons of punishment are empty for the crowd when error possesses it.
But good, patient with us, and slow to punish,
the almighty Lord will hurl no wrath
unless he first warns and knocks on hardened hearts,
stirring up the foreseeing prophets by his august mind.
And now the Lord had commanded Jonah to foretell
to the Ninevites the destruction they deserved; but he, knowing
that the Lord spares the submissive and remits deserved punishment
to suppliants and is easily moved to kindness, put off going,
lest he prophesy in vain, when the threats gave way to peace.
Soon his plan is flight — if there is any such possibility —
to avoid God and escape the Lord's right hand,
beneath which the whole trembling world is held in check.
Or is there some reason in what the prophet does from his holy heart?
On the lip of the shore, most famous for its trusty harbour,
lies the city of Joppa, facing the coasts of Cilicia.
From there, then, Jonah hastily seeks Tarsus by ship,
across the waters of the same God; nor indeed is it strange
if, fleeing the Lord on land, he found him on the waves.
For suddenly a tiny cloud had stained the air,
stirred up as a sulphurous fleece from the seed of the wind,
and little by little, giving birth to a great mass, it closed with the sun
and shut in the cheated day with a host of darkness.
The sea becomes the mirror of the sky; a black ring stains
the waves; the heavens plunge into darkness and the sea rises,
and there is nothing in between, as the billow touches the clouds,
the halls of the winds, all of which it mingles in its whirlwind.
Fury from every quarter gnashed at the fugitive Jonah.
A single ship was the prize contested by sky and sea;
it is battered this way and that; all its timber trembles under the
wave-breaking blows; below, the spine of the shaken keel
quivers; the yard, straining and creaking, shudders on high;
the mast itself bends, wavering, about to snap.
Meanwhile the sailors, groaning in fear, try everything
for the ship and for their lives: to pay out the coils of the anchor,
to unlace the undergirding cable, to strain at the rudders,
to haul at the straining ropes, to push the windlass round with their chests;
some in turn strenuously bail out the well of the inner sea,
heavy with stench; then the cargo and all the load
they hurl overboard, and strive to overcome peril by loss.
Then come wretched cries at every crash of the sea,
and they stretch out their hands to the powers of gods that are nothing,
whom the might of sea and sky does not fear, drowning them no less,
stowed away in the stern, in its angry whirlwind.
Unaware of all this, the guilty man himself, beneath the hollow vault of the stern,
was resounding with snoring sleep through his puffed nostrils,
even then, in his sleep, shaping a figure of the Lord.
Him, as he slept in calm peace, proud in his repose,
the man who directs the work of the wave-cleaving prow
pressed upon and shook: “What,” he says, “in such peril
are you singing dreams through your nose? In so great a storm do you alone
have a harbour? Look, [?] covers us; our only hope is in the gods.
You too, whoever your God is, offer vows and prayers,
and calling upon him as a suppliant, bend your ancestral deity.”
Next, who is nearest to the guilt, who is the cause of the storm,
they resolve to learn by lot; and the lot does not lie about Jonah.
Then they question him: “Who are you, from where among men, of what estate,
of what people, of what home are you called?” He confesses that he is the servant,
one who deeply fears the God who raised the heavens on high,
who laid the earth, who poured out the whole [?] in its body;
and he reveals that he is his fugitive, and the reasons why.
They froze with fear: “What fault of ours, then, is this to you?
What will happen now? By what means shall we calm the waters?”
For the savage seas were swelling more and ever more.
Then the Lord's prophet, at the prompting of the Spirit, begins:
“See, I am the tempest, I am the whole madness of the world;
because of me,” he says, “the sky falls upon you and the sea rises,
because of me the land is far, death is nearest, there is no hope of God.
Rather, cast the cause of it headlong, and lightening the ship,
throw this one great burden into the willing sea.”
But they strive in vain to turn their course
back toward land, for the rudder would not let itself be turned,
nor would the stiff balance of the yard be shifted.
At last they cry to the Lord: “Do not give us over into the jaws of death
for the sake of one soul, nor will that we be spattered
with innocent blood, if this is where your right hand leads.”
And now there, rising from the deepest gulf, a sea monster,
rolling the scaly train of its shell-encrusted body,
pressed the waves closer, the marble sea shaken,
seizing by God's will the prey which, tumbling forth
from the height of the stern, it swallowed in its slimy jaws,
and hurried the living feast down into its long belly,
and together with the man it devoured the rage of sky and sea.
The waves of the sea are laid flat, the shadow of the sky dissolves.
Here the waves, there the breezes become friendly again,
and as the calm keel marks out a safe path,
white tracks blossom in the blue furrow.
Then the sailors joyfully, with reverent fear, offer the Lord
sacrifices of thanks, and then enter friendly harbours.
The prophet Jonah sails too, taken aboard another
vessel, and cuts through the waves beneath the deepest waves,
sailing in bowels, while a beast's breath breathes around him,
enclosed, yet not wet with water, inside the sea and outside it,
among half-eaten fleets and bodies dissolved
by putrid digestion, now on the point of learning his own funeral.
But since he was one day to be a sign of the Lord,
he was not meant for destruction, but to be a witness of death driven away.
IV. TO A SENATOR WHO HAD TURNED FROM THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION TO THE SERVICE OF IDOLS.
When I saw you once again devoted to strange and empty
rites, and held fast by the old error,
I was shaken with astonishment. Since you have always loved poems,
I hastened to write verses, answering you in verse,
to rebuke you. For to prefer darkness to light —
who would put up with that? That you should believe the Great Mother
can be called a goddess, and think once more that she must be worshipped,
whose worshippers are branded with foul disgrace?
For her priests, in women's tunics,
confess by their outward dress the vice within,
and think lawful what is not lawful. So through the city
they mince along, speaking in softened voices,
and hold their weary loins with an outstretched thumb,
and change their own sex by a notorious crime.
And when they celebrate their rites, they declare that on those days
they are chaste. But if they are chaste only then,
as they claim, what are they for the rest of the time?
And because they are forced to be pure at least once,
they rage in their minds, tear their bodies and pour out their blood.
What kind of sacred rite, really, is the one that goes by the name of "Blood"?
Now I have also learned that it was not age that made you
bald, but your religion, and that, with the Gallic boot put aside,
your feet are bound in soft papyrus.
A thing astonishing enough, a fall from the very height!
If a consul came out of the temple of Isis into the city,
he would be a laughingstock. And who would not laugh at you,
that you, who were once a consul, are now a servant of Isis?
And that what shames one in the first rank does not shame you in the second,
and that you degrade your talent with base hymns,
while the crowd chants back to you and the senate tears you to pieces,
and that you, once painted with the fasces in your own house,
now also wear a dog's face and carry a sistrum.
Is this humility? It is the image of humiliation.
Those memorials will remain in your house forever.
Public rumour has also reached our ears
that you said: "Goddess, I went astray; forgive me; I have come back."
Tell me, if you can: when you often made such pleas
and begged for pardon, what words did she speak to you?
Truly you have lost your mind, you who follow the mindless.
You repeat these things again and do not feel that you are sinning.
See what you deserve: perhaps you would be less to blame
if this were all you knew and you remained in this error;
but since you have entered the doors of the law that cherishes truth,
and it has been granted you to know God for a few years,
why do you hold on to what should be abandoned, or abandon what should be held?
You worship nothing while you worship everything, nor do you consider in your heart
how the true differs from the false, how light differs from shadows.
You play the philosopher, though your opinions keep changing:
for if the people's anger should turn your stomach,
you will become a Jew as well, and be thought wholly unstable.
Pay heed to what I say: lofty wisdom does not please.
Everything that is excessive turns into its opposite: heat and cold
produce the same effect — this one burns, and so does that.
So darkness takes away sight, and so does the sun shining in one's face,
and an icy bath and a scalding one do equal harm.
The body is nourished by food, the body is ruined by food,
and anything stretched beyond its measure lessens its own power.
Again, if you sit, it is a great rest from toil;
if you sit too much, it is toil. For Virgil the poet
set it down as a punishment: "He sits, and will sit forever,
unhappy Theseus." What is useful, if prolonged, always does harm:
long lunches do harm, long fasts wear one out.
So too much wisdom makes a fool. "A wicked sect" [?] —
so the goddess taught me; she called moderation lovely. [?]
But you care neither for a sect nor for moderation.
A steady mind, however, is overturned by no surge of passion,
and simplicity itself never plots any evil.
Hence sincere faith will enjoy an everlasting dwelling,
while deceit, on the other hand, will be tormented in long-lasting fire.
Choose what you want, so that you may escape the punishment you deserve.
Yet, I say, let the believer earn this pardon on these terms:
just as it will be a light offence if you refuse to learn the truth,
it will be no light offence if you abandon the truth once known.
But perhaps ripe old age will correct you
and call you back to better things, once you have had your fill of these errors;
for time changes evils, time sets all things in order.
So then, when a wiser age has brought you back,
learn to keep faith with God, lest you happen to fall
into the same stumbling twice; for this saying is true:
whoever does not know how to avoid a second time the stone his foot struck
and carelessly bruises his limbs again
should blame himself and not blame any chance.
Correct your offence by faithfulness, correct your mind.
It was enough to sin once; stop being afraid:
he will not be guilty who repents of what he was before.
V. ON EASTER
There is a place which we believe to be the centre of the whole world;
the Jews call it Golgotha in their ancestral tongue.
Here, I recall, a tree cut from a barren trunk
was planted and bore wholesome fruit;
yet it did not give its fruit to those husbandmen who had planted it:
strangers received its blessed fruits.
This is the form of the tree: it rises from a single trunk
and soon stretches out its arms into twin branches,
as yardarms spread full and heavy sails,
or like a yoke when the bullocks have been unhitched from the plough.
The fruit it bore, which fell as its first ripe seed,
the earth conceived; and soon from it (wonderful to tell!)
the third day had raised up once more a branch, awesome to earth and to heaven,
blessed with life-giving fruit.
For twice twenty days it grew steadily [?]
to an immense height, touched heaven with its topmost crown,
and at last hid its holy head on high,
while it put forth twelve branches of enormous weight
and, spreading them, stretched them out over the whole world,
so that they might give all nations food and everlasting life
and teach how death itself can die.
Then, when fifty days had run their course,
from the topmost summit the breath of the heavenly Spirit
brought down into the branches a draught of divine nectar;
the leaves, heavy with sweet dew, dripped on every side.
See! Beneath the vast shade of the canopy of branches
there was a spring; here, calm and disturbed by no mishap,
with clear, unclouded waters, while the grasses around
poured forth bright colours from flowers of every kind.
Around it countless nations and peoples gathered,
how varied in race, sex, age and rank:
maidens and wives together, widows and young brides,
infants and boys, men, youths and old men.
Here, when they saw the branches bending down, weighed with fruits
of many kinds, they rejoiced to touch with eager hands
the fruits moist with heavenly nectar.
Yet they could not pluck them with their longing hands
until they had wiped off the filthy, muddy traces of their former way
and washed their bodies in the holy spring.
So for a long time, walking round about on the soft grass,
they gaze up at the fruits hanging on the lofty tree;
then, if any husks have fallen from those branches,
and sweet fruits dripping with abundant nectar,
they eat them, longing to taste the true fruits.
And so, when their mouths have received the heavenly savour,
they change their hearts and begin to lose their greedy minds
and to know what it is to be human through a sweet sense.
We have seen the unfamiliar savour turn many a stomach,
and the poison of gall stirred up by the honey,
so that they rejected the good savours with troubled minds,
or, having eagerly taken it, did not love it, and after
keeping it down badly for a long while, at last vomited up the taste.
Yet often many, with renewed minds,
have restored their sick spirits, and endured what they had said they could not,
and reaped the fruit of their labour.
Many, too, who dared to touch the holy springs
suddenly went away again and, slipping back,
wallow once more mixed in the same filth and mire.
But many, carrying the truth in a good heart,
receive it with their whole souls and store it deep within.
And so all who are able to approach the sacred springs
the seventh day sets beside the longed-for waters;
they dip their fasting limbs in the clear springs.
Thus at last they lay aside the filth of mind
and the stain of their former life, and bring back from death pure
and shining souls, destined to go to the light of heaven.
From here the road leads to the branches and the sweet fruits of salvation;
from there the road leads to heaven through the branches of the lofty tree.
This is the tree of life for all who believe. Amen.
VI. TO FLAVIUS FELIX, ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD
I, who once in song called upon the Muses of the countryside,
and hailed the breezes rosy with the flowers of spring,
and the heavy ears of the summer harvest,
who cut the swelling grapes from autumn's vines
and always praised the peaceful olives of winter,
and drew tuneful waters from the springs,
and sang of woods leafy above the straying grass:
now I will at once tune my song to the heavenly regions of light;
now let me reach the Muses who bring the light,
to reveal the nymphs hidden at the river's source
and the glad woods set beneath another star;
and with them I will tell in song of the eternal flames:
whence the boundless sea surges into swelling waves,
what power bids the solid earth to tremble,
and whence golden light first shone upon the new world;
who could have fashioned man from the fertile clay,
whence a race could grow in an empty age,
and what varied desire for life the peoples have;
what first offspring of death was begotten by evil,
whence comes the sweet scent and the blush of rosy garlands,
what makes the vine swell with glad grapes,
and how the new barley grows milky on tender stalks,
how the tree ripens its black olives in the frost,
who gives increase and vigour to the varied shoots
and shields the mother of her offspring with soft shade.
It is good to know all the beginnings of the branches,
so that through all things we may come to know the true God,
who made the light, the seas, the heaven and the earth,
and adorned the new world with varied stars,
and first bade the cattle and the birds come forth,
and granted that the waters of the sea be filled with fish,
and made the sands teem with living creatures.
Such songs will I draw out, once the Muses are set in order,
and I will pour forth wholesome water from new springs,
and the glad rain that comes from gentle clouds,
flowing freely and deep into the souls of men;
I will catch it in full streams upon our fallow fields.
Come now, reach the untroubled, living spring,
and quickly drink the easy-flowing water of life.
If anyone wishes to escape the punishments of eternal flame,
unaware [?] of the day and ignorant of the age to come,
and to win instead the rewards of a righteous life,
let him remember this one God and pray to him alone,
who set the whole world in the balance beneath his threshold,
abiding eternally and ever to be through the ages,
holding all the ages, and alone before the ages,
God unbegotten, without end, who alone holds the divine throne
and ever towers above the high heaven,
alone almighty, whom all things obey,
[Father, Son and Spirit, who are ever one,]
who formed man, pleasing to himself, for all time,
made him shepherd of the cattle, lord of the wild beasts,
and gave him the right to rule the birds, the sea and the land;
he who by speech alone could stretch out the heavens,
and by a word commanded the solid earth to hang in space,
and quicker than it could be said divided the waters of the sea,
loved to fashion with his hands this cherished form,
and willed that his own fair image should dwell in it,
and with his Spirit breathed the breath of life upon its face.
Lest man, forgetful of God, should rashly dare so much
and touch anything beyond the warning, one thing —
the fruit by which he would know evil and discern the right —
he at once forbade him to touch: the forbidden fruit.
How great the gifts of the world that God allowed to man!
He set upon him the most sweet pledge of his love,
gave him useful and dear commandments for his salvation,
placed under his rule the lands and every living soul,
the feathered race, the cattle, every kind of wild beast,
and the race of the sea, all creatures that swim.
But since, transgressing the law by the first crime,
the first man straightway set aside the Lord's commands,
at his wife's urging to every evil he perished by death.
For woman first committed the evil of sin,
and betrayed her husband and lured him from the law.
Eve, wickedly persuaded, opened the gates to death,
and wrought funerals for herself and for her whole race.
Hence (unhappy wickedness!) death flowed forth for all time.
From then on crime spread easily and ran deep,
and the farmer's toil drove the year more harshly on.
The cunning serpent brought this about through wicked envy.
From then on the many evils committed by the peoples
brought forth unspeakable seeds through wicked deeds.
And therefore God alone, who holds the highest power,
who occupies the topmost heights above the lofty heaven,
dwelling on high for ever in light unapproachable,
mindful of the past and foreknowing what is to come,
keeps for ever the judgement each generation has deserved:
and all the souls that sluggishly govern bodies
and move man by the reason that ranges through his limbs,
as soon as they depart, laying aside the weight of the limbs,
and go forth light, loosed from earthly bonds,
and seek again their own regions in different places —
straightway some are shut up in hidden darkness,
but others are at once recalled to glad airs,
kept safe for the rewards decreed by the law,
until the bodies rise again [?] with their limbs restored:
then men will pay the interest on their first life,
and stand before God's judgements, mindful of the past,
each awaiting his own punishment for his own crime.
Or do they perish utterly, like cattle, without name [?] weight [?] breath,
or in ending pour out God's breath in vain [?]?
Can God almighty, by whose nod
all things are ruled, not restore life after death?
Or does the Lord seem unable to do anything at all?
If he could shut off the bright light from the darkness,
and could compose the whole mass of things by a word,
and make all things out of nothing with his mighty voice,
why could he not from something put together the familiar
shape that once had been, that had lived before,
and bid it rise again in the likeness of its own form?
Since all things are God's, the earth will all the more give back all things
at his command; it will call back whatever it once covered.
If perhaps flame consumed someone laid to rest on the pyre,
or the sea cast someone down into its blind waves,
if a fish's belly sated its hunger on anyone,
or wild beasts dealt cruel deaths to limbs,
or the blood lay where birds tore the body away:
not even these last deaths will withhold anyone from the Lord;
they must appear before God alive from death,
and men must stand having taken back their own forms.
So dry seeds are entrusted to the turned earth
and rot, dead, deep within the furrows;
then the stalk comes to life with its ears renewed,
and grows strong and golden again with living grain,
and new harvests rise with varied yield.
All the stars will set, and, reborn, will shine again;
the day dies with its light into thick night,
and night perishes into day as things are uncovered by the light,
and lofty day rises again among its stars.
The sun sets, bearer of splendour, with its bright light on high;
the light dies as evening comes and shades the world,
and returns and renews joy for the whole age:
so the phoenix, burned, lives again from its own death,
and the bird at once rises from its pyre.
And the tree stripped of its leaves buds in its season
and once more bends its branches with fruit from the bud.
Therefore, when the world trembles at the divine voice,
and the powers of the high air are shaken to their depths,
then comes an unheard-of crash and the mightiest rumblings of heaven,
as God advances, as the judge of the world comes:
at once innumerable ministers rush together to go,
and surround God with heavenly majesty;
angelic hosts descend far and wide in throngs.
All are God's messengers, to whom belong divine power
and surpassing beauty, all of them spiritual powers.
Fiery is their vigour, gleaming their bodies;
the divine might of heaven flashes forth: from it the whole sky thunders,
from it the whole earth, trembling to its depths, bellows back,
in labour with the men she will be bound to give back at the command.
The companions marvel, the clouds at last are thrown into turmoil,
the stars in amazement suddenly quake at the power from on high,
as God gives the command, easily, with the voice of the Mighty One.
At once the tombs burst open throughout every kingdom,
all the ground pours forth bones through gaping chasms,
and the opened sand belches out living peoples.
Limbs cling to [?], bones are knit with marrow,
and sinews bound together govern breathing bodies,
and the veins, filled once more with blood, begin to move,
and the souls that had been sent away are restored to the opened hollows;
all the rising organs seek again their own places.
(O wondrous faith!) Hence every generation springs up;
the throng of the dead springs up from the ancient dust.
Mothers and men rise again to the light regained;
great-hearted youths, boys and unwedded girls,
and old men long dead stand there with living souls,
and the groaning world resounds with the wailing of infants.
With them the various nations come from their deepest abodes,
the band of the East and those whom the farthest land beholds,
those who dwell in the middle zones beneath the sloping sky,
and those who hold the Rhipaean heights beneath the frosty star:
every inhabitant of every region is there, trembling,
peasant and soldier, kings with their diadems laid aside,
the rich mingled with the poor in one equal host.
Deep trembling everywhere; now the world groans with prayers,
and the peoples, stretching out their hands, cry out in wonder.
The Lord himself is seated, bright with towering light,
and, all-powerful, he flashes as fire amid all the powers,
and gleams on his lofty throne in the heavenly seat,
hedged about by martyrs, a shining company of men,
and he stands forth attended by his blessed prophets,
whose bright brows shine with snow-white fillets.
And now the priests are present in shining garments,
bearing gleaming crowns, the rewards of life,
and all, kneeling with bended knees, worship:
"Hagios, holy, God alone!" is the one cry of all.
Then the Lord will bid the twofold people take their stand:
he commands that the righteous be separated from the number of the wicked,
and bids them, clothed with strength now that death is conquered,
to possess for ever a breath of light that cannot be quenched,
to walk through ancient realms that ever flourish,
through rich groves and ever-pleasant meadows,
and to live an everlasting life in a glorious body.
There is a place beloved of the Lord on the Aeolian shores,
where clear light shines and a more healthful breeze blows,
an eternal day and an unchanging season,
a region set apart for God, very rich in plains,
an abode surpassingly blessed beneath a cloudless sky,
where the air is ever glad and will ever be in light,
and a gentle wind breathes life-giving gusts.
The rich earth yields alike from its all-bearing soil:
purple blooms blaze across the level meadows.
All things, gleaming brightly, ungrudgingly mingle their light;
one glad flower clothes another with its light as with a cloak.
Here the rosy fields are varied with snow-white seed,
and the snow-white fields ripple with rosy flowers.
You could not tell with which flowers the fields are more beautifully sweet,
or with which they breathe more happily in the heavenly air,
which is finer in beauty or which excels in honour.
Never are such lilies born in our flowering gardens,
nor have such ever bloomed in our fields;
our familiar rose does not so redden, nor the white so open,
nor is purple so steeped in Tyrian red.
Gems shine beautiful with many-coloured stones:
here the prase glistens, there the carbuncle burns,
and the emerald pours out its flashing light.
Here too cinnamon grows on fragrant sprays,
and glad amomum breathes its scent from green leaves.
Here lies native gold of radiant light,
and lofty groves reach to heaven with flowering crowns,
and the richest buds weigh down the green branches.
No India ever spread out groves like these;
the green pine does not raise its tops so thickly,
nor does the tall, swaying cypress so curl its foliage,
nor does the branch in spring blossom better in its season.
Here dark [?] woods flourish otherwise upon the lofty heights,
and they alone stay green for ever, untouched by hail.
No leaves fall, no flower fails in its season:
the treetops grow green, firm in their strength [?], and the tree blushes purple.
But that flower, I think, is a rose, with an even blush upon it,
so sweet a beauty of scent does it breathe from its petals.
A most beautiful tree stands with blossom and new fruit,
and the fruitful trunks are thick with life-giving produce.
Rich honey breathes its fragrance from the green boughs,
and milk fit for drinking flows in brimming streams.
Whatever the holy earth makes green breathes life there;
whatever flowers from the bud brings blessing too,
and the very soil is fragrant with fair and healing clay.
A spring there floods the fields with a gentle stream,
and from it four rivers water the divided land.
There, I think, the sky, clothed in flowers, keeps perpetual spring.
No cold under a wintry star changes the breezes,
nor does summer blaze with radiance and oppressive heat;
heaven tempers the calm breezes with its own light
and refreshes the fruitful earth with a kinder breath.
There is no night there; the stars hold off their darkness;
wrath and treachery are absent, and dire greed;
fear is shut out and cares are driven from the threshold.
The wicked man is banished from here, an exile to the farthest regions,
and toil is forbidden to touch these blessed borders.
Here the faith of old rests in its chosen seat.
Justice lives rejoicing in an everlasting covenant,
and secure salvation rejoices in the peaceful fields,
ever to live and ever to be in light.
Here is whoever was a devout cultivator of the just and the good,
who feared God, the Thunderer, with a guiltless mind,
and honoured his parents with sacred devotion,
and lived always a holy life free of crime;
or who, as often as he could, comforted the needy with friendly wealth
and came to the aid of the poor in their great distress,
helper of the poor, wont to rescue orphans,
who rescued the injured and aided those weighed down by accusations,
who gave his guests the cherished tokens of his table,
who performed all his duties according to the divine commands,
harmed no one, and coveted nothing that was another's:
they all, exulting in praises of God
and praying together, raise their voices to the stars;
singing psalms to the Lord, they give thanks with joy,
and will go on the blessed way with angels as their escort.
After the Lord has bestowed these happy gifts
and sent the righteous together into the eternal kingdom,
lo, the wretched throng comes, lamenting its crimes:
there is groaning; all mourn with burning tears
and confess their deeds with constant howling;
they tremble at the fiery darts that bear down on them as they deserve.
Now the angels seize them and forbid them to pray,
and forbid them to pour out belated words of repentance,
and now, as the flame draws near, pardon for their prayers is refused.
O wretches, how often was the divine power
made known to you, how often the majesty of the True One revealed?
You heard the thunder, you saw the lightnings of heaven,
you constantly knew the rains and the wrath of winds and hail,
and how often the nights and the calm days:
the fruitful seasons brought you the gifts of God,
spring gave roses in abundance, summer did not lack its grain,
autumn offered its varied mellow fruits,
and icy winter always pressed the glad olives.
God gave everything, and no goodness was lacking,
yet through all this the whole human race did not know God.
The earth trembled before God, the sea stood still at God's nod,
and the river, trembling, flowed back over dry sands,
and all creation joyfully confesses God in all things.
Yet you denied this Lord of heaven and earth,
and instead put the righteous to death with cruel slaughter,
and many of you often drove God's heralds away.
Among you the truth was always held to be a crime.
And therefore you will reap the fruit of a wicked sowing:
behold, you do not know the day that you are wont to mock.
You will go into the deep darkness of fire and sulphur,
to suffer in burning the savage wrath amid your pains.
These the Lord bids depart to eternal punishment,
to go beneath the burnings of Gehenna for ever without end,
to be driven in a mass through the seething pools of flame.
In his threatening he bids the elements turn to flame,
and all the fire of heaven to descend from the clouds.
Then greedy Tartarus shoots forth its swift fires,
and the seas will surge with stormy flames,
and the whole earth will mingle the living with its embers,
and the angry air will brandish furrows of flame,
and the scorching world will be armed with every torch,
and with hellish onslaught the fires will seize the world.
Driven headlong, they are swept up into the blaze;
they flee this way, and from that way are swiftly driven back.
The savage wrath of the flame meets them as they flee,
and now at last they recognize their punishment for their crime.
And now, where the land is held by no tiller,
and is pressed down by the sea's farthest bounds in the deep,
where the sun, its course run, marks the limit of the sky,
and the risen stars are hidden when they have crossed the world,
the air grows thick with dense darkness, the light shut away;
there lie the last pools, flaming with hidden streams.
The nature of the place is fiery, with punishments appointed,
and the swamp of hell, glowing with heat in its depths,
thunders with horrors, a sea of punishment; a furnace
seethes and, flaming, is churned by a swift whirlpool,
a river rushing into torments with a surging flood;
all the scorched sand is mingled with the mire.
Hither the groaning, captive throng of the wicked will be sent,
and the host of sinful bodies, doomed (O horror!) to burn.
Great is the lamenting there, weeping joined with outcry,
and a swift gnashing; then the howling of the sufferers
will rise far off out of the flame, and the loud groaning
of the fire and of the burning will mount into the resounding air.
Then the human race pays for the evils it committed,
and they will begin to stretch out belated prayers to heaven,
and will now wish to know the God whom they would not know.
There each will confess the savagery of his life,
his guilty hands and his mind made cruel by crime,
and will bear witness to the unspeakable savagery of his life.
First, whoever before had thought wrongly of God
and worshipped wayside stones as false divinities,
and consecrated altars bloodied before images,
and feared painted figures that have no voice,
and adored the flimsy shadows of a false deity;
and whoever was straightway led astray by wicked error;
anyone who was an adulterer, whoever had killed his children,
anyone who lived with a mind conscious of any evil,
or had gone about robbing, or defrauding a client;
anyone who stained his hands with human blood
and mixed poisons that bring a hidden death;
then anyone who hid his thefts in a hollow heart,
or rejoiced in wicked gain from another's misfortune;
whoever committed any wickedness whatever:
deep burning will torment them with bitter fire,
and all will pay the penalty in a living death,
so [?] the whole mourning throng of men.
How often did the holy prophets sing of these things,
often warned by the Spirit of God, foretelling what was to come?
[No one (wretched!), no one, alas, lent an ear.]
Thus God almighty willed that his rewards be known,
and the threats of the law laid down [?] through such things,
by sending many to proclaim heavenly words.
At last, by God's command, the prophet joined the bones together,
and was astonished at the tombs suddenly moved, not of themselves;
bodies that had lain [?] in the clay, their ashes scattered,
he marvelled then to see rise alive as the breath came into them,
and with their voices stretch out their hands to heaven.
[And they give thanks for such things to God and to Christ the victor.]
They indeed returned to their silent tombs,
and withdrew to be kept for God's day to come:
for a little while he bade them be held in their deep resting places,
until that great day, when the time is fulfilled,
shall come. All of you, acknowledge the true Lord,
who alone can make the soul strive toward the light,
and who can likewise thrust it down into the Tartarus of punishment,
and to whom all power over life and death lies open.
For God, to will is enough to be able, and by speaking it is done.
He alone is to be feared by me in my inmost heart.
And since every course is brought to a close by death,
whoever lives today will carry his own life with him.
And therefore, while life remains, while you may enjoy the light,
while you may repent, before the end of time
overtakes you unawares and closes your unknowing eyes —
that last day, which is held by the law of death —
first of all, in what time remains, keep watch for your precious salvation,
and readily and steadfastly turn your course toward the good.
After your errors and your sins, suppressed by holy rites [?],
after you whom the wandering storms have tossed too long,
take the straight paths and hold to the favouring winds.
From now on, first drive out crime with glad hearts,
and let the guilt long hardened be washed from your breast;
then, made gentle, blot out the unspeakable evils you have committed,
and appease the awesome God with unceasing prayers;
let all the worst things give way to the good, mortal things to the living.
Keep now the new life free from crime,
and keep your minds devout and in the true name,
and as suppliants ask pardon for your former offences.
Now let pure hearts ripen in devout cultivators;
lift up innocent hands in righteous prayers,
and readily offer your voices in praise of God.
Let your minds begin to grow used to what is good and true,
and let the gifts of the divine law be celebrated all the more,
and remember good deeds and at once take them up.
Let the sordid evils once committed lose their worth for you,
and all better things will glow for you who are devout,
and life is set free at once from dreadful perils,
and will come to the eternal rewards for which it prayed.
